alignments.note: Illative ὅτι rendered by the verse-opening For.
Ordinary conditional particle to if. The ASV writes if and any one as separate words, so rule 39's compressed εἴ τις → whoso is not this case and the pair splits under rule 2.
Indefinite τις to any one; rule 17's generic-noun clause heads on any rather than on the supplied one, as rule 69 heads any man on any.
Copula expressed in the Greek, so it stands on its own word.
Anarthrous noun, so the supplied a is an ordinary rule 51/7 helper on the noun it determines.

λόγου is anarthrous, so no article competes for the determiner: rule 51 makes the supplied the a helper on the noun, and the case preposition of rides with it under rule 21's determinerless clause. Head on the noun per rule 17.
Expressed conjunction to and.
Ordinary negative to not; no negative indefinite stands with it, so rules 41 and 59 are not in question.
Anarthrous noun with supplied a as a rule 7 helper.
Substantival demonstrative rendered by the pronoun he; no article governs it, so rule 49 is not in question.

ἔοικεν to is like, headed on the lexical predicate like rather than the copular auxiliary under rules 9 and 17. Competing reading: taking is like unto whole here, on the ground that like unto reads as one English phrase; I put unto with ἀνδρί instead, because it realizes that noun's dative case, which is rule 36's refusal to read a preposition off a phrasal verb applied to a case-marked complement.

Dative complement of ἔοικεν. The case preposition unto and the supplied a ride with the noun: no Greek article stands here to anchor them under rule 21, so rule 21's determinerless clause and rule 51's anarthrous clause both leave them on ἀνδρί.
Attributive participle rendered by the bare participle beholding.

Article of πρόσωπον. The ASV recasts the face of his birth as his natural face, so the English determiner slot is occupied by the possessive his, which belongs to the genitive αὐτοῦ under rule 20. The article realizes nothing.
Bare face, its determiner having gone to the possessive under rule 20.
Article of γενέσεως. The ASV turns the genitive into the attributive adjective natural and writes no determiner for it, so the article has nothing to anchor under rule 23.
γενέσεως rendered adjectivally as natural; the ASV's own note records the Greek as the face of his birth.

Genitive pronoun carrying the English possessive, which is what empties the article of πρόσωπον under rule 20. The pronoun is free — the ASV has spent it on nothing else — so rule 76's second arm does not apply.
Expressed preposition to in; the ASV spreads the phrase over separate words, so rules 45 and 94 do not join it to its noun.
Anarthrous noun with the supplied a as a rule 51/7 helper.

review_notes: Reviewed and returned unchanged: I could not find an edge or a head the contract decides differently. All 20 source ids and all 27 target ids are partitioned exactly once; every aligned unit has nonempty arrays with both heads inside them, and the two unrepresented units are source-only with a valid source head and a null target head.

The one materially contested edge is unto in he is like unto a man. The accepted reading keeps it with ἀνδρί as the dative's case preposition, and I confirm it. Rule 42 refuses in as many words to read a supplied preposition as part of the governing word's own idiom merely because nigh unto reads as one English phrase, and like unto is the same shape; rule 69 is the closer model still, giving οὐ κατενάρκησα οὐθενός → on any man to the governed word with the case preposition riding along under rules 21 and 36. The competing reading — is like unto whole on ἔοικεν — is named in that unit's note and remains defensible.

Both three-token units on a single noun (of the word, unto a man) are driven by the Greek being anarthrous, not by bundling. λόγου and ἀνδρί have no article, so rule 51's anarthrous clause makes the supplied the and a helpers on the noun and rule 21 has no article for the case preposition to ride with. Had an article stood there, rule 21 would have split of the and unto a off onto it.

The two unrepresented articles are decided by different rules and should not be collapsed into one reason. τό before πρόσωπον is rule 20 displacement: the ASV's recast puts his in the determiner slot and αὐτοῦ is present and unspent, so rule 76's availability arm does not reach it. τῆς before γενέσεως is rule 23: the genitive becomes the attributive adjective natural and the ASV writes no determiner for it at all.

ἔοικεν heads on like rather than is. The Greek is a single finite verb of resemblance, so the English is is the auxiliary rule 9 and rule 17 both tell us to pass over in favour of the lexical predicate. The expressed οὗτος keeps its own he, so no supplied-subject question under rules 53 or 68 arises here.
